notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material for every verse. The gaps were in parts 2 and 3. I didn't find teachers who disagree along denominational lines, so the debates below are between individual commentators. I also found nothing on Genesis 42 from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, catholic.com, oca.org or any prosperity or hyper-grace teacher, so those are left out. The search tool hit its limit before I could look further. Two sources were only partly read: the Pulpit Commentary page cut off around v. 19, and on the Enduring Word page (David Guzik) I read the full text up to about v. 27 and only summaries after that.

---

## Part 1: Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik thinks Jacob saw a strange look on his sons' faces when Egypt came up, because they knew Joseph had probably been sold there. Their consciences hurt whenever Egypt was mentioned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/
- The Pulpit Commentary disagrees. It reads the look as helpless indecision and says there is no need to see guilt in it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- An older note on Bible Hub's v. 1 page sees the sons as careless and helpless, each one expecting relief from the other. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42.htm

**v. 2**
- Poole says "I have heard" explains the "saw" of v. 1. "Go down" fits geography, since Egypt lay lower than Canaan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-2.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) comments that God would not interpose miraculously when natural means of preservation were within reach. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-2.htm
- Pulpit infers that the family's flocks had been badly reduced by the drought. It also sees God's plan in Jacob sending his sons rather than servants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- Guzik's application is that God uses material need to push people toward things they would never normally do. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**v. 3**
- Pulpit gives two possible reasons all ten went: safety, or because grain was rationed per person, so more buyers meant more grain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm

**v. 4**
- Pulpit says Benjamin was kept home not because he was young (he was over twenty) but because he had taken Joseph's place in his father's heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- An older note explains that Benjamin is called "Joseph's brother" because they shared both father and mother. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-4.htm
- Guzik says Jacob lived in constant fear of losing Rachel's other son. His comment: if only Jacob could trust the hand of God he could not see. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**v. 5**
- Pulpit takes "among those who came" to mean they travelled in a caravan or arrived among others in the same need. It says the repeated mention of the famine opens a new section and is not, as some critics argue, a sign of a different author. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit notes that the Hebrew word for "ruler" means someone with absolute authority. Joseph probably set prices and inspected foreign buyers rather than selling grain himself. The brothers' bowing fulfils his dream from Genesis 37. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- Guzik's point: the brothers sold Joseph to defeat his dreams, but by sending him to Egypt they made the dreams come true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/
- Catholic voice (Ambrose, on Joseph's grain policy in general): Joseph preferred to sell the grain rather than to give it to the hungry. For if he had given it to a few there would have been none for most. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/34012.htm

**v. 7**
- Pulpit says Joseph spoke harshly not out of revenge but to reach their hearts and learn how they now felt about him and Benjamin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- Guzik says Joseph acted under the Holy Spirit's guidance; this was not revenge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**v. 8**
- Pulpit lists why they didn't know him: twenty years had passed, plus his high rank, Egyptian manners and foreign language. Joseph knew them because they were already grown men when he last saw them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- Barnes adds his shaven head and beard and his Egyptian clothes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/42-9.html
- Guzik sees a picture of Jesus here: Jesus saw who we are long before we see who He is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**v. 9**
- Ellicott says every traveller in the East faced suspicion of spying, and Egypt especially distrusted Semitic peoples. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-42.html
- Commentators disagree on what the land's "nakedness" means:
  - Pulpit, Keil and the Cambridge Bible say its unguarded borders and defences. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-9.htm
  - Barnes says the opposite: how poor the land had become in the famine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-9.htm
  - Coffman follows the scholar E. A. Speiser: the word is a figure for military secrets hidden from enemies. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/genesis-42.html
- Guzik thinks Joseph might have revealed himself at once if it had been up to him, but God brought the dreams to mind and guided him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**vv. 10–12**
- Barnes and Pulpit: no father would send ten sons together on a spy's dangerous errand. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- Pulpit cites Candlish: Joseph's harshness hid his growing weakness of heart, not cruelty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-9.htm
- Trapp says Joseph spoke as a test, not as his real opinion, and this way got news of his father and Benjamin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/gen-42.cfm

**v. 13**
- Commentators split on "one is no more." Pulpit lists the views:
  - Keil: proof they had not yet truly repented.
  - Wordsworth: a suppression of the truth.
  - Lawson: an outright lie.
  - Pulpit's own view: after twenty years it was a reasonable guess.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- Guzik calls it a lie the brothers knew was a lie. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**v. 14**
- Ellicott thinks Joseph wanted Benjamin in his power and may not have minded punishing his brothers somewhat. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-42.html
- Pulpit says Joseph knew they weren't spies; he kept up the charge to bring them to a right state of mind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm

**vv. 15–16**
- On the oath "as surely as Pharaoh lives," Pulpit notes that Calvin found Joseph somewhat to blame for it. Others treat it as just a strong way of speaking. The demand to bring Benjamin was meant to find out the truth about him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm

**v. 17**
- Pulpit says the three days gave the brothers a taste of what they had made Joseph suffer. It also shows his mercy: three days for them against his years in prison. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- Guzik makes the same contrast and says the days made them think about their sins. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**v. 18**
- Pulpit notes Joseph said "God" (Elohim) rather than the LORD's name, which would have given away his Hebrew background. The point was to show he would not condemn them on mere suspicion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- Guzik says Joseph wanted them to trust him, not fear him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**vv. 19–20**
- Pulpit notes the plan is reversed: one brother is held instead of nine. Quoting Keil, it contrasts Joseph's care for their hungry families with their leaving him in the pit to starve. It lists several suggested reasons for demanding Benjamin, including Wordsworth's view that God was leading Joseph without his knowing it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- Guzik: they were not truly "honest men" while the hidden lie about Joseph remained. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**v. 21**
- Guzik takes it as a good sign that they linked their trouble to their sin so quickly; they must have thought of it often. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/
- Pulpit notes the narrator never told us Joseph pleaded with them, but their guilty memories did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- The Expositor's Bible says their position now mirrored Joseph's. It warns that being aware of sin is not the same as repenting of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/genesis/42.htm

**v. 22**
- An older note says Reuben rightly rebukes them: murder was intended, and when he was sold his death was pretended. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-24.htm

**v. 23**
- Coffman suggests that overhearing this told Joseph that Reuben had tried to restrain the others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/42-23.html
- Guzik says the interpreter hid the fact that Joseph spoke Hebrew. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**v. 24**
- Ellicott: Joseph had no bitterness and melted at their regret. He likely chose Simeon as the one most guilty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-42.html
- Poole: his tears were partly pity and partly joy at seeing them face their sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-24.htm
- Why Simeon? The commentators differ:
  - JFB, Gill and Poole think Simeon was probably the ringleader, pointing to his violence at Shechem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-24.htm
  - The Cambridge Bible says he was simply next oldest, with Reuben spared. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-24.htm
  - Clarke repeats a rabbinic tradition that Simeon was the one who bound Joseph. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/42-24.html
  - Constable thinks Reuben was passed over because Joseph overheard v. 22. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/42-23.html
  - Guzik says we don't know; perhaps Simeon volunteered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**vv. 25–26**
- Guzik sees the returned money as a picture of Jesus giving to people before they are reconciled to him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/
- An older note suggests Joseph could not bear to take money from his father. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-24.htm

**v. 27**
- Ellicott: the "lodging place" offered at most walls and water. Tradition says Levi opened the sack. He also says the Hebrew uses different words for "sack" and "bag." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-42.html
- Barnes: this was probably their first night's stop on a six- or seven-day journey. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bis/genesis/42-9.html

**v. 28**
- Ellicott translates the Hebrew literally as "their heart went forth": their courage left them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-42.html
- Guzik (Spanish edition) says a guilty conscience doesn't even know how to handle God's gifts. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/genesis-42/

**vv. 29–34**
- Guzik: this time, unlike twenty years earlier, they told their father the truth. Yet "one is no more" was still a lie. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/
- Constable quotes a writer who says they softened the news, making Simeon sound like Joseph's guest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/42-37.html

**v. 35**
- The Cambridge Bible says this verse highlights how hard their position was: the money had come back and Simeon was a prisoner. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-35.htm
- An unlabelled older note on the same page suggests they had found the money earlier and hidden the fact from Jacob. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/42-35.htm

**v. 36**
- Ellicott: in Hebrew the things are "upon me," burdens to bear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-42.html
- Commentators differ on whether Jacob suspected his sons:
  - Gill thinks Jacob suspected them of harming Joseph. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/42-36.html
  - JFB disagrees, and adds that even a good man struggles to submit to Providence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_042.cfm
- Guzik: Jacob spoke more truth than he knew. His despair came exactly when God was arranging the rescue. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/

**v. 37**
- Ellicott and Gill: Reuben was offering a strong pledge, not expecting his sons to be killed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-42.html
- Clarke sees honesty and love in the offer. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/42-37.html
- Others are critical:
  - Matthew Henry calls the offer foolish and notes Reuben never said "if the Lord will."
  - Constable calls it "pathetically weak."
  - Coffman ties it to Reuben being "unstable as water" (Genesis 49:4).
  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/42-37.html
- Calvin calls the offer exceedingly barbarous. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/42-36.html
- Guzik: what Reuben offered as a gesture, God actually did by giving his Son. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/genesis/genesis-42.cfm

**v. 38**
- Ellicott: "grave" is literally Sheol. Jacob had probably lost Leah too, and losing Joseph, in whom Rachel seemed to live on, crushed him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-42.html

## Part 2: Where interpreters differ

These are disagreements between commentators, not clearly between denominations. The one label I saw on a page was StudyLight tagging Gill as "Calvinist."

- **Joseph's motive (vv. 7–24).**
  - Guzik: Joseph was guided by the Spirit to bring his brothers to repentance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-42/
  - Ellicott: Joseph may have felt indignation and been willing to punish them a little. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-42.html
  - Expositor's Bible: Joseph was cautious and judged them like any shrewd man would. The test that finally proved their repentance (the cup in Genesis 44) was applied without his intending it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/genesis/42.htm
- **Other contested verses:** v. 1 (guilt or just helplessness), v. 9 (defences or famine), v. 13 (lie or reasonable guess), v. 15 (whether the oath by Pharaoh was wrong), v. 24 (why Simeon) and v. 37 (Reuben's offer). See the notes above.

## Part 3: Other views

- **Critical scholarship (reported only as Pulpit rebuts it).** Pulpit argues against critics who see the repetitions in v. 5, or the late-sounding word in v. 6, as evidence of different authors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/42.htm
- **Dispensational reading.** William Kelly reads the story as prophecy about Israel: no deliverance for Israel until "Joseph and Benjamin are united." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/42-37.html
